title: Continuous annealing of medium-Mn steels: Plasticity controlled by SIMT kinetics through grain size distribution and Mn concentration in retained austenite
abstract: Intercritical annealing, a process widely employed to achieve a high fraction of retained austenite in medium-Mn steels, typically requires several hours, resulting in low economic efficiency. Alternatively, flash annealing, characterized by high heating rates, relies on induction heating, which introduces technological complexity and limits industrial applicability. Both methods are considered either economically inefficient or technically challenging to implement on a large scale. In this study, a novel continuous annealing method is proposed, designed to be compatible with existing industrial installations. This method enables the production of steel with a significantly improved UTS × TEl product. Compared to conventional intercritical annealing, the proposed method produces a lower Mn enrichment of austenite. However, the retained austenite exhibits significantly finer lath thickness, tuning its stability. This structural modification facilitates an intense and gradual martensitic transformation across the entire deformation range, contributing to improved strain hardening and plasticity. The analysis also reveals a strong correlation between the strain hardening behavior of the steel and the calculated stability of the retained austenite. These findings provide a detailed description of the kinetics of strain-induced martensitic transformation, offering valuable insights into the material’s plastic performance.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Steels containing between 3 and 12 wt% of Mn (Medium-Mn) have received increasing attention in the automobile industry due to their great potential for cost-effective applications in manufacturing responsible autobody parts [ 1 , 2 ]. Thanks to the combination of high ultimate tensile strength and total elongation (UTS x TEl > 20 GPa%), they may replace dual phase steels in the future for crumple zone elements [ 3 ]. The production of such high-plasticity sheet steels is mostly done through intercritical annealing (IA), during which the initial fresh or tempered martensite partially transforms to austenite through the austenite reversed transformation process (ART). During this process both C and Mn atoms diffuse from martensite to the austenite, which enhances its thermal and mechanical stability [ 4 , 5 ]. Final strain hardening and thus mechanical properties of intercritically annealed Medium-Mn steels depend on a matrix strength and a fraction and mechanical stability of retained austenite (RA), with the latter strongly depending on its chemical composition, size and morphology [ 6 , 7 ].

The conventional approach to the intercritical annealing of Medium-Mn steel assumes heating the steel to the equilibrium temperature range allowing to obtain the largest fraction of stable austenite (often between 650 and 680 °C [ 8–10 ]). Next, soaking takes place, which usually lasts for several or even several dozen hours [ 8 , 11 ], followed by final cooling at a different rate. A long soaking time is required to obtain a high proportion of austenite enriched in C and Mn at an equilibrium temperature. However, this is associated with softening of the matrix [ 12 ] and austenite grain growth [ 13 ], which decreases the RA stability [ 14 ]. This type of treatment can be conducted with existing batch annealing installations, but it is neither an economical nor an efficient method of steel production. Due to the sensitivity of the steel to local annealing conditions, there is additionally a serious risk of obtaining non-uniform properties depending on the distance from the coil core [ 15 , 16 ] as microstructure and mechanical properties of Medium-Mn steels are highly sensitive to the annealing time [ 17 ].

For economic and technological reasons, attempts were made to accelerate the intercritical annealing process. Works on the so-called flash annealing [ 18 ] – involving heating rates up to 100 °C/s to over 800 °C followed by the immediate quenching – confirmed the possibility of obtaining a high strength-plasticity relationship in such treated materials. In this method a high fraction of stable RA is ensured by C enrichment and severe grain refinement as the redistribution of Mn is negligible [ 19 , 20 ]. However, this type of process requires a very efficient heating method, such as induction heating, which significantly limits the possibility and range of its industrial implementation.

To address the market demand for an industrially feasible and economically viable process for producing medium-Mn steels using existing infrastructure, this study investigates a novel continuous intercritical annealing method for such sheet steels. The research aimed to determine the optimal heat treatment parameters for continuous annealing conditions that yield the best mechanical properties, based on broader studies. The results were then compared with a heat treatment variant previously applied to the tested steel in earlier studies [ 21 , 22 ], which had provided the best mechanical properties under batch annealing conditions. This comparison enabled a clear evaluation of the mechanical properties achieved through both types of industrial heat treatment. The objective was to assess the feasibility and justification for annealing medium-Mn steels in a continuous process. Furthermore, a comprehensive analysis of the factors influencing mechanical properties in both cases allowed for the identification of a correlation between the steel’s ductility and the strain-induced martensitic transformation (SIMT) occurring during plastic deformation, which is governed by grain size distribution and manganese concentration in RA. Both of these aspects represent the novel contributions of this study.

sections.heading: Material and methods
paragraphs: The steel with the chemical composition of 0.16C-4.7Mn-1.6Al-0.2Si-0.2Mo (wt.%) was subjected to investigations in this study. The increased manganese concentration causes a high hardenability of the steel and significant delay in the onset of its phase transformations such as ferritic, pearlitic or bainitic, both during cooling [ 23 ] (critical cooling rate) and also in the case of isothermal holding [ 24 ]. This causes that during cold rolling, usually the microstructure of the steel is either martensite or tempered martensite [ 25 ] − in the case when high tempering is applied – as the typical ferritic-pearlitic microstructure is not possible to be obtained [ 23 , 26 ]. It was reported that due to usually a low C concentration in medium-Mn steels they show moderate cold formability [ 27 , 28 ] under such microstructural conditions.

The final microstructure and mechanical performance of the material depend on whether intercritical annealing is performed on hot-rolled (without cumulative deformation) or cold-rolled (with cumulative deformation) steel. In the former case, during intercritical annealing, only austenite grains nucleate and grow along the martensite grain boundaries. This results in a lath-like microstructure, which leads to continuous yielding during tensile testing, with minimal or no dynamic strain aging effect. This is particularly important for automotive applications [ 4 ]. In contrast, when samples are annealed immediately after cold rolling, the cumulative deformation is relieved through recrystallization during annealing. This produces a microstructure of equiaxed grains, which exhibits discontinuous yielding with large yield point elongation, potentially causing significant issues with the repeatability of manufactured components [ 29 ]. Therefore, after cold rolling, additional austenitization is often applied to obtain a final, non-deformed martensitic microstructure, similar to that of hot-rolled material [ 10 , 11 , 30 ]. This is an additional, expensive thermal cycle, which is a departure from the typical process of plastic and thermal processing of automotive steel. However, no other method of eliminating discontinuous yielding in these steels − limiting their potential industrial implementation − has been developed so far.

In order to demonstrate the highest possible mechanical properties during the tests, steel with an initial non-deformed martensitic structure ( Fig. 1 
                      a) corresponding to the state immediately after hot rolling or cold rolling and austenitizing was used for the tests. The 4.5 thick steel plate was selected to enable producing normalized ø4x10 mm dilatometric samples according to ASTM A1033-04 [ 31 ].

The heating rate of 3 °C/s was selected on the basis of work [ 32 ] to prevent diffusionless austenitic transformation, which may occur at fast heating rates and deteriorates stability or RA. Simultaneously, the selected heating rate can be achieved using conventional continuous annealing lines for DP sheet steels [ 33 , 34 ]. Physical simulations of continuous intercritical annealing were conducted using dilatometry (Bahr DIL805A/D). In order to investigate the effect of annealing time corresponding to the continuous process range, a soaking time range from 2 to 120 s was chosen. Previous studies [ 21 ] have shown that soaking for 60 s at 680 °C or lower (the temperatures typically used for medium-Mn steels in batch annealing) results in low mechanical properties (UEl < 14 %, TEl < 18 %). It is due to the small fraction of very stable austenite. Therefore, in the current study, an annealing temperature range of 680–760 °C was selected to produce a larger fraction of austenite and reduce its stability to an optimal value in terms of SIMT kinetics. Based on these tests, the sample annealed at 710 °C for 40 s (sample CIA) was chosen for further analysis, as it exhibited the highest mechanical properties (strength-plasticity product) among all tested variants.

In addition to confirming the possibility of achieving high mechanical properties in medium-Mn steel heat-treated under continuous annealing conditions, the aim of this study was also to compare these properties with those of steel treated under conditions similar to batch annealing. Based on the previous studies on batch annealing of medium-Mn steels [ 3 , 21 , 22 ], the intercritical annealing conditions of 680 °C and 3600 s (1 h) were selected as a reference of standard – batch IA (sample SIA) as the best in terms of the obtained elongation and the strength-plasticity product.

The high hardenability of the tested steel – due to the increased Mn concentration [ 23 ] – affects its insensitivity to cooling conditions, allowing it to be cooled in air after IA. Air cooling of plates up to 5 mm in thickness corresponds to a cooling rate of about 1 °C/s, which was used in physical simulations. The complete processing routes are plotted in  Fig. 1 b.

Microstructure of the steel was characterized using scanning electron microscopy (SEM − Zeiss Supra 25 with EBSD detector), transmission electron microscopy (TEM−S/TEM TITAN 80-300) equipped with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDXS). The thickness of RA laths was measured using ImageJ software on high-resolution SEM images, what is the accepted method for multiphase steels with non-equalized grains [ 35–37 ]. At least 300 RA laths were measured for each sample. Sub-size tensile specimens with a gauge length of 9 mm and a cross-section of 3 x 3 mm were cut along the hot-rolling direction. Next, they were heat-treated using a modified DIL805 dilatometer, which ensured the precise control of time and temperature. Static tensile tests were performed using ZWICK Z020 testing machine at a strain rate of 0.001 s −1 . The elongation was measured by an extensometer. sections.heading: Microstructural characterization
paragraphs:
Microstructures of steel after both standard and continuous annealing variants are very similar as seen in  Fig. 2 
                         . They are composed of ferritic matrix (darker phase) with very fine lath-type RA (bright laths). Both microstructures are homogeneous with locally occurring thicker ferrite laths developed from larger laths of martensite – RA nucleates preferentially at boundaries of the martensitic laths [ 41 ]. Fresh martensitic structures in intercritically annealed medium-Mn steels are located within the RA laths, as they form from unstable austenite during final cooling or even during deformation-related sample preparation, such as cutting or grinding. These martensitic structures can be distinguished from austenite by their morphology. After nital etching, martensitic areas exhibit an inhomogeneous, “rough”, lath-like substructure [ 42 ], while stable RA shows a homogeneous, bright appearance [ 4 ], as seen in  Fig. 2 . The fresh martensitic areas were not observed in either of the samples. The CIA sample shows a marginal fraction of carbides in the structure ( Fig. 2 b,d), which may indicate a slightly lower degree of its tempering than in case of the SIA sample, where carbides are not present ( Fig. 2 a,c). However, these differences are not reflected in the hardness of both samples, which are almost identical (∼296 HV1). The SEM observations indicate a higher amount of RA in the SIA sample, which was also confirmed by XRD studies. It contains ∼3 wt% more RA (37.1 %) compared to the CIA sample (34.4 % of RA). The RA lath thickness measurements performed on the SEM images at high magnifications ( Fig. 2 c,d) indicated noticeably thinner RA laths in the CIA sample (148 nm on average). In the SIA sample the RA laths have a thickness of 172 nm on average (16 % more). The detailed distribution of lath thickness in both samples presented in  Fig. 3 
                          reveals that in case of CIA sample an increased frequency of grains with a thickness of 130–170 nm is present. Together they constitute over 55 % of all grains. The grains thinner than 130 nm and thicker than 170 nm reach ∼15 and ∼29 %, respectively. In case of SIA sample the RA grain with the thickness of 130–170 nm constitute ∼38 % of all grains. Thinner and thicker grains constitute 14 and 48 %, respectively. No fresh martensite was observed in any samples.

Fig. 4 
                          shows the detailed EBSD analysis of the microstructure of the CIA sample. In the ferritic matrix, in the vicinity of austenite (alpha phase), there are no darker areas with low Image Quality values, which could suggest the presence of fresh martensite [ 43 , 44 ]. This confirms the full stability of austenite during heat treatment, observed using SEM. The grain boundaries with an angle of ∼45° are dominant as seen in  Fig. 4 a,b. They correspond to the characteristic misorientation correlation (K-S and N-W) between austenite and ferrite [ 45 ]. They constitute more than 85 % of all grain boundaries ( Fig. 4 c), which indicates a very high homogeneity of the microstructure as the ferrite-ferrite (previous martensitic laths) boundaries with an angle higher than 50° [ 46 ] constitute only about 10 %. The IQ profile marked by double-arrowed black line in  Fig. 4 a and presented as a chart in  Fig. 4 c indicates that the IQ value, which corresponds to the density of lattice imperfections [ 47 ] is high in ferritic regions and decreases after reaching RA regions. It suggests that RA has a higher dislocation density than ferrite.

The TEM analysis was performed to investigate the chemical partitioning during soaking ( Fig. 5 
                         ). The 3600 s of soaking at 680 °C resulted in an increase of Mn concentration from the bulk 4.7 to about 7.4 wt% on average as one can see in  Fig. 5 a. However, also in the sample soaked at 710 °C for only 40 s a significant Mn redistribution occurred, as austenite contains about 6 wt% of Mn, which gives an increase of 1.3 wt% in just 40 s ( Fig. 5 b). This contradicts some reports that claim that many hours of annealing are necessary to redistribute manganese [ 48 , 49 ] and supports another works indicating the high Mn enrichment during shortened intercritical annealing [ 21 , 50 ]. The carbon concentration, determined based on XRD results, is 0.44 % ± 0.02 for the SIA sample and 0.46 % ± 0.03 for the CIA sample. Both values are very similar, with the slightly higher carbon concentration in the CIA sample likely caused by a smaller fraction of RA. This results in the constant carbon content being distributed over a smaller fraction of austenite [ 4 ].

Further analysis of TEM images confirmed a more frequent presence of thinner RA laths in the CIA sample ( Fig. 5 b), observed by SEM. The RA regions in TEM images are darker than ferritic ones indicating a higher density of dislocation in RA suggested by EBSD ( Fig. 5 c–d).

For a more systematic characterization of the RA, a number of grain thickness and their Mn enrichment measurements were conducted. The results presented in  Fig. 6 
                          indicate a significant difference of Mn concentration in RA between samples after both variants of heat treatment. This difference is clear regardless of their RA lath thickness. For the SIA sample it is about 7.2 Mn wt.% and for the CIA it is about 6.1 Mn wt.%. An interesting observation is the fact that despite the different thickness of RA in the range of ∼50 to over 200 nm in a given sample, the Mn concentrations in RA laths are at a very similar level. The trend line visible in  Fig. 6  indicates a slight decrease in Mn concentration with an increase in the thickness of the Mn strip; however, it is negligibly small. A similar trend was observed for both samples despite completely different soaking times. The comparison of the measurements with the TEM results presented in works [ 51 , 52 ] confirms these observations. During long intercritical annealing time, Mn diffusion from ferrite to austenite takes place, which results in continuous sluggish increase in average concentration of this element [ 21 ]. Moreover, it leads to local concentration of Mn in the areas of RA close to the interphase boundary [ 4 , 53 , 54 ] due to the slow diffusion of Mn in austenite [ 54 ]. In the present case, due to the short annealing time it is not possible to enrich austenite by diffusion from the surrounding grains. This suggests that the increased concentration of this element is caused by the nucleation of austenite itself at the martensite-martensite boundaries as Mn and C tend to segregate into these areas [ 55 , 56 ]. Medium-Mn steels, due to their high hardenability, typically exhibit a martensitic microstructure after hot and/or cold rolling. During heating to the intercritical annealing temperature, the martensite undergoes tempering, which leads to the formation of carbides highly enriched in Mn, preferably at grain boundaries [ 57 ]. The synergy of these mechanisms results in the formation of austenite with a lath-like morphology during annealing [ 58 ] observed in  Fig. 2 . This is attributed to the increased concentration of austenite-stabilizing elements and the presence of carbide precipitates, which act as nucleation sites for austenite along martensite boundaries [ 59 ].

sections.heading: Mechanical performance influenced by stability of RA
paragraphs:
The mechanical properties of the samples after standard (SIA) and continuous (CIA) intercritical annealing are compared in  Fig. 7 
                         . Both samples exhibit beneficial continuous yielding due to their initial martensitic structure, which ensures recrystallization-free annealing [ 4 ]. Similar to hardness, the yield strength (YS) of both samples is comparable, with the CIA sample reaching 655 MPa and the SIA sample 683 MPa ( Fig. 7 a). Strain hardening is more pronounced in the CIA sample, resulting in an UTS of 1050 MPa with a uniform UEl of 24.8 %. In contrast, the UTS and UEl for the SIA sample are 894 MPa and 21 %, respectively. The TEl is also slightly higher for the CIA sample, reaching 34.7 %. This results in a UTS × TEl value of 36.4 GPa%, for the CIA sample, compared to 30.4 GPa% for the SIA sample, representing an improvement of approximately 20 %.

Fig. 7 a also presents the mechanical behavior of samples soaked for 40 s at different temperatures. When soaked at temperatures below 710 °C, the mechanical behavior is similar to that of dual-phase [ 60 ] or ferritic/pearlitic steels [ 61 ], which do not contain RA. At the higher temperature of 720 °C, more intense strain hardening occurs compared to the sample soaked at 710 °C; however, this is accompanied by a decrease in plasticity, indicating low stability of the RA. Based on these observations, the sample soaked at 710 °C was chosen as optimal.

A better understanding of the plastic deformation behavior is provided by the changes in the instantaneous strain hardening exponent (n), shown in  Fig. 7 b. For the SIA sample, a moderate and continuous increase in the n value is observed, reaching 0.2 at a true strain of 0.19. This trend is generally favorable for mechanical properties, as it indicates a gradual and constant transformation of RA to martensite, which improves both strength and plasticity. In contrast, for the CIA sample, the n exponent is significantly higher throughout the entire range of uniform deformation, reaching up to 0.29 at a true strain of 0.17, which is 30 % higher than that of the SIA sample. This behavior and the differences in mechanical properties between the samples are closely related to the RA transformation kinetics, which are also depicted in  Fig. 7 . For the SIA sample, the RA transforms gradually, and even after reaching the UTS, there is still more than 10 wt% of RA in the microstructure. In the case of the CIA sample, a much larger fraction of RA transforms to martensite during straining. At a strain of about 0.17, the RA fraction stabilizes at approximately 4 wt%. This phenomenon is reflected in the n exponent, where, in the true strain range of 0.17–0.2, its value plateaus and then begins to decrease due to the lack of stress-induced martensitic transformation (SIMT). This suggests the exhaustion of the TRIP effect. The significantly higher RA fraction at the UTS point for the SIA sample (∼5 wt% more RA) can be attributed to its high initial mechanical stability, local stability redistribution caused by grain size differences, and further stabilization during straining, likely due to grain fragmentation, as noted in previous studies [ 3 , 21 , 22 ].

To precisely analyze the observed differences in the SIMT effect, the Ms temperature range of RA in both samples was calculated using Formula 4, based on the redistribution of lath thickness ( Fig. 3 ) and their enrichment in Mn ( Fig. 6 ). The results in  Fig. 8 
                          show the RA stability (expressed as the Ms temperature) as a function of RA lath thickness. The RA stability is presented as a range due to varying Mn concentrations, measured by TEM EDXS, in different grains ( Fig. 6 ).

The specific Ms temperature values depend on the formula used and may differ significantly when other equations or experimental results are applied, as shown in [ 21 ]. Moreover, the stability of austenite is influenced not only by grain size and chemical composition but also by crystallographic orientation [ 62 ], the strength of neighboring phases [ 63 ], and other factors. Therefore, in this type of analysis, the focus should be on trends in temperature changes rather than absolute values.

In  Fig. 8 a, the changes in RA stability (marked by three points for each RA lath thickness: maximum, average, and minimum) are plotted against lines representing the RA thickness distribution in the samples. It is evident that due to the significantly higher Mn concentration in the SIA sample, the Ms temperature for a given lath thickness is lower by 20 to 50 °C, indicating higher RA stability in the SIA sample.  Fig. 8 b presents the same data as  Fig. 8 a, but the RA lath thicknesses are now correlated with their stability (Ms temperature). This correlation allows for determining the relationship between the frequency of RA grains in the microstructure and their stability, making it easier to analyze and compare the theoretical kinetics of RA to martensite transformation. Grains with the highest Ms temperature will begin transforming first during deformation.

For the SIA sample, due to the higher stability of RA, the transformation theoretically starts at a lower temperature (45 °C), but it proceeds very gradually. The maximum RA (∼15 wt%) starts to transform to martensite at around 1 °C. In contrast, for the CIA sample, the martensitic transformation is predicted to start at 65 °C (20 °C higher than for the SIA sample). As temperature decreases, a rapid increase in the fraction of RA grains transforming to martensite is expected, with the maximum fraction (20 % RA) beginning to transform at a theoretical temperature of 19 °C.

Since the thermal and mechanical stability of RA are interrelated, it is possible to compare the RA stability graph ( Fig. 8 b) with the changes in strain hardening ( Fig. 7 b) of the analyzed samples. The trends in both graphs are similar. For the SIA sample, there is a moderate and gradual increase in the n value, which aligns with the gradual transformation of RA to martensite as the temperature decreases. In contrast, for the CIA sample, both the n value increases rapidly with strain progress and a significant fraction of RA transforms to martensite as the temperature decreases. These observations align with the experimental changes in RA observed in  Fig. 7 b.

The analysis of the results clearly indicates that, despite the lower initial RA fraction in the CIA sample, it achieved higher TEl and, especially, UEl, along with a higher UTS. The broader distribution of RA grain sizes in the SIA sample—and thus a broader range of RA stability—should theoretically result in a more gradual SIMT and improved mechanical properties. However, in the case of the SIA sample, SIMT kinetics is not fast enough. As a result, despite progressive RA transformation, necking occurs at the UEl of approximately 21 %, while over 10 % of RA remains, which is too stable to transform under the applied strain. The strain hardening provided by RA transformation was insufficient to delay necking further. Although SIMT continues within the UEl–TEl range due to increasing deformation, this deformation is confined to the necked region, causing the SIMT effect to diminish in the rest of the sample.

Assuming two samples where all RA transforms to martensite before necking, the sample with a higher initial RA fraction should exhibit superior mechanical properties—both tensile strength and uniform and TEl. However, experimental results indicate that the stability of RA and the resulting SIMT kinetics play a decisive role. In the CIA sample, despite its initially lower RA fraction, faster SIMT kinetics enabled a greater extent of RA transformation, resulting in higher strain hardening, which is clearly reflected in the superior UTS value. This inhibited the localization of deformation, as the martensite formed strengthened the material at its “weakest areas,” delaying neck formation. Although both samples exhibit similar TEl—a result of continued RA transformation in the necked region—the more critical industrial parameter is the UEl, which is notably higher in the CIA sample.

The obtained results clearly suggest that optimizing the heat treatment of medium-Mn steels requires careful adjustment of both the RA fraction and its stability. A high RA fraction alone does not guarantee superior mechanical performance. For the SIA sample, processed under batch annealing-like conditions, the variant with the best strength–ductility balance was selected, representing the optimal combination of RA fraction and stability. In contrast, the CIA sample—despite undergoing a significantly shorter heat treatment—achieved an even better balance of these factors, as evidenced by its superior mechanical properties.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: Significantly different mechanical properties were obtained regardless that microstructure and RA fractions obtained in Al-alloyed medium-Mn steel samples annealed at 680 °C for 3600 s in batch annealing mode and at 710 °C for 40 s in continuous annealing mode appeared to be alike. This enabled the analysis to be carried out on distinguishing the role of RA stability and the kinetics of the SIMT in shaping the plastic properties.

The sample subjected to continuous intercritical annealing exhibited manganese enrichment of 6 wt%, which is 1.4 wt% lower than the sample annealed in the standard manner. However, this was offset by the much finer RA grains in the continuous annealing sample, where the average RA grain thickness was 148 nm compared to 172 nm in the standard annealed sample, characterized additionally by a wider range of grain size distribution. The synergy of RA grain size and chemical composition in continuously annealed sample enabled the transformation of 30 out of the initial 34 % of RA within the range of homogeneous deformation, which allowed to obtain a UEl of almost 25 %. It was due to the presence a significantly larger number of grains with lower stability compared to the standard annealed sample, facilitating a gradual but very intense SIMT effect and significantly improved plasticity-strength properties.

In the standard annealed sample, RA also underwent a gradual martensitic transformation, but to a lesser extent, due to the higher stability of RA grains. Due to the transformation of a smaller fraction of RA, necking occurred earlier compared to the continuously annealed sample, resulting in a UEl of only 21.3 % despite the initial RA content of 37 %. The reduced activity of the SIMT also led to a decrease in UTS by more than 100 MPa. The change in the stability of RA—resulting from the grain size distribution and chemical composition of the sample—was linked with the kinetics of phase transformation. This approach enabled a precise analysis of the SIMT effect and provided an explanation for the resulting mechanical properties, which represents the novelty of this work.

TEM analysis revealed a novel observation that the RA thickness did not significantly influence its Mn enrichment after both heat treatment variants. Despite a large variation in RA thickness (50–250 nm), the differences in Mn concentration were less than 0.5 wt%, which contradicts previous assumptions from other studies.

Another key finding, and the primary novelty in response to industrial demands, is the confirmation of the feasibility and justification for annealing medium-Mn steels in a continuous mode. The research demonstrated that high mechanical properties (UTS of 1050 MPa, UEl of 24.8 %, and TEl of 34.7 %) can be achieved using process parameters compatible with existing industrial lines. Moreover, it was shown that continuous annealing can lead to significantly improved mechanical performance (by 20 %) in comparison to the conventional batch annealing process, along with a reduction in soaking time from 3600 s to 40 s (approximately 98 % reduction). Considering the entire process (heating, soaking, and cooling), the time is reduced by 78 %, from approximately 4380 s to 960 s.
